paragraphs: Skeptical Opinions, It Is Important to Remove to a Distance the Objects of Human Actions

In ages of faith, the final end of life is placed beyond life. People of those ages therefore naturally, and almost without intending it, grow used to fixing their gaze for many years on some unchanging object toward which they constantly move. They learn, by imperceptible degrees, to suppress a multitude of petty passing desires so as to be better able to satisfy the great and lasting desire that possesses them. When these same men engage in the affairs of this world, the same habits show in their conduct. They tend to set some general and definite aim for their actions here below, and all their efforts are directed toward it. They do not run from day to day after some new object of desire; they have settled designs that they never tire of pursuing. This explains why religious nations have so often achieved such lasting results. While they were thinking only of the other world, they discovered the great secret of success in this one. Religions give men a general habit of conducting themselves with the future in view. In this respect they are no less useful to happiness in this life than to felicity hereafter, and this is one of their chief political characteristics.

But as the light of faith dims, the range of man’s vision shrinks, as though the end and aim of human actions seemed to come within his reach more every day. Once men have allowed themselves to stop thinking about what will happen to them after life, they readily slip into a complete and brutal indifference to the future, which is only too much in keeping with certain propensities of mankind. As soon as they lose the habit of placing their chief hopes on distant events, they naturally seek to gratify their smallest desires without delay. No sooner do they despair of living forever than they are inclined to act as if they would exist for a single day only. In skeptical ages, therefore, there is always reason to fear that men may give way continually to their casual daily desires, and that, renouncing altogether whatever cannot be obtained without prolonged effort, they may establish nothing great, permanent, and calm.

If the social condition of a people in these circumstances becomes democratic, the danger I am pointing out grows greater. Everyone is constantly striving to change his position. An immense field of rivalry is thrown open to all. Wealth is amassed or squandered in the shortest possible time amid the turmoil of democracy. Under these conditions, visions of sudden and easy fortunes, of great possessions easily won and lost, of chance in all its forms, haunt the mind. The instability of society itself feeds the natural instability of man’s desires. Amid these perpetual fluctuations of his lot, the present swells in his mind until it hides the future from his sight, and his looks reach no further than tomorrow.

In countries where, unhappily, irreligion and democracy exist together, the most important duty of philosophers and of those in power is to keep striving to place the objects of human actions far beyond man’s immediate range. Confined by the character of his country and his age, the moralist must learn to defend his principles from that position. He must work constantly to show his contemporaries that, even amid the perpetual commotion around them, it is easier than they think to conceive and carry out long-term undertakings. He must teach them that, although the face of mankind may have changed, the methods by which men can provide for their prosperity in this world are still the same. He must teach them that among democratic nations, as elsewhere, the general and unquenchable passion for happiness can be satisfied only by resisting a thousand petty selfish passions of the moment.

The task of those in power is just as clearly marked out. At all times it is important for those who govern nations to act with the future in view, but it is even more necessary in democratic and skeptical ages than in any others. By doing so, the leading men of democracies not only make public affairs prosper; they also teach private individuals, by their example, the art of managing private concerns. Above all, they must strive as far as possible to banish chance from the sphere of politics. The sudden and undeserved promotion of a courtier makes only a passing impression in an aristocratic country, because the nation’s institutions and opinions taken together habitually force men to advance slowly along tracks they cannot leave. But nothing is more pernicious than similar displays of favor before the eyes of a democratic people. They give the final push to the public mind in a direction where everything is already hurrying it onward. In times of skepticism and equality especially, the favor of the people or of the prince, which chance may bestow or withhold, ought never to take the place of attainments or services. It is desirable that every advancement there should appear to be the result of some effort, so that no greatness comes too easily and ambition has to keep its gaze long fixed on an object before it is gratified. Governments must set themselves to restore to men that love of the future which religion and the state of society no longer inspire in them. Without saying so, they must teach the community in practice, day by day, that wealth, fame, and power are the rewards of labor — that great success lies at the far end of long desires, and that nothing lasting is obtained except by toil. When men have grown used to foreseeing from afar what is likely to happen in the world and to living on hopes, they can hardly keep their minds within the exact circumference of life, and they are ready to break through the boundary and look beyond. I do not doubt that, by training the members of a community to think about their future condition in this world, one would bring them gradually and unconsciously nearer to religious convictions. Thus the means that allow men, up to a certain point, to do without religion are perhaps, after all, the only means we still have of bringing mankind back, by a long and roundabout path, to a state of faith.
